1380.title: Side by side, closed
1380.howItsDone: Buddhists across the schools use the dharma wheel as a sign of the teaching, and some temples and centers mark the anniversary of the first teaching, recalling the wheel set rolling in the deer park.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your door among the schools: Dasama's burning house, and a door to walk through rather than a wall to build. Your line was a home, not a wall.

Kondanna is sitting in a deer park with four old companions, listening to the man they once walked away from. The talk is still going when something comes clear for him: whatever arises also passes away. Then, the Pali account says, a shout goes up. The earth spirits cry out that the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling, and that no one in the world can stop it. The cry is passed up from one heaven to the next, until the whole universe shakes. The discourse is named for that moment: setting the wheel rolling.
screen: `FIVE OLD COMPANIONS.` → `KONDANNA SEES IT.` → `THE WHEEL IS ROLLING.`

segments.voice: This block set the schools side by side, and today it closes, so walk the wheel once more. First, the hub: what all share. The four truths and the eightfold path. The three jewels: the Buddha, the teaching, the community. Precepts, meditation, kindness. Second, the spokes that differ. The three turnings, a Mahayana map. The arahant, honored in Theravada, and the bodhisattva, honored in the Mahayana. One Buddha or many. Buddha-nature, inborn or grown. Emptiness and not-self. Rebirth, taught and questioned. Lay and monastic. Devotion and meditation. Sudden and gradual. Third, the rim, where the wheel touches the road. Three canons, four languages, robes in saffron, maroon, gray and black. Festivals on different days for one birth. Councils where the schools meet. The reason this path ranks none of them, and the door you might call home. Fourth, the picture. Tradition reads the eight spokes of the dharma wheel as the eightfold path, which you met as eight spokes back in year two. Spokes point in different directions and need each other to make a wheel. Take one out and it wobbles. Hold them all to the same hub and it rolls. The cry in the deer park said no one could stop the wheel. It didn't say it would roll in only one land, one language, one color of robe. Next, a new block: the practice traditions, the chants and sittings and walks each school does with its body.
screen: `THE HUB: WHAT ALL SHARE.` · `THE SPOKES THAT DIFFER.` · `THE RIM ON THE ROAD.` · `MANY SPOKES, ONE WHEEL.` · then, large: `ONE WHEEL.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, name one school you've met and let a little thanks go toward it: Theravada, with its forest monks and morning chants; Zen, with its silence and breakthroughs; Tibetan Buddhism, with its maroon robes and long canon; Pure Land, with its chanted name. You don't need to agree with each one, only thank it for the people it has carried.
Side by side. The schools of Buddhism set next to each other, each taught in its own terms, none ranked: different spokes on one turning wheel. Today's word.
Your line: one wheel. Many schools, one hub. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.

1381.title: Chanting in Pali
1381.hook: the morning chant of Theravada monasteries: homage, refuges, reflections
1381.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks, nuns and lay visitors chant in Pali at morning and evening services, opening with homage to the Buddha said three times, then the three refuges, then reflections, often from memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, side by side: the schools on one wheel, a shared hub and different spokes, and the block closed. Your line was one wheel.

It's still dark. A wooden bell sounds across a monastery courtyard, and figures in robes cross to the hall, barefoot, carrying small lights. They kneel in rows facing a Buddha image, laypeople from the village behind them. Someone in front draws a breath and sings out a single line, and the whole room picks it up, low and even, like a river finding its bed. Nobody looks at a page. A new block begins today, the practice traditions, with the sound that opens the day.
screen: `A WOODEN BELL IN THE DARK.` → `KNEELING IN ROWS.` → `ONE LINE, THEN ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: In the order heard in some Theravada monasteries, the morning chant moves in three steps. First, homage: "Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa." Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the fully self-awakened one. By custom it's said three times, slowly, and it names the Buddha by three qualities, not by a personal name. Second, the refuges: "Buddham saranam gacchami. Dhammam saranam gacchami. Sangham saranam gacchami." To the Buddha I go for refuge, to the teaching, to the community. Then again, opening with dutiyampi, a second time, and with tatiyampi, a third. You met the three jewels earlier this year; here they are in the mouth, before breakfast. Third, the reflections. Chanting books vary from monastery to monastery, but a common one comes from the Buddha's own advice in the Numerical Discourses: five facts to recall often. I am subject to aging. I am subject to illness. I am subject to death. I will be parted from everyone and everything dear to me. My actions are my own, and I will inherit them. It sounds heavy for the morning. Some teachers say the opposite: it makes the day lighter, because nothing in it comes as a surprise. Why Pali, if the room speaks Thai or Sinhala or Burmese? These are the words the tradition has kept, and a monk from Sri Lanka and a nun from Thailand can chant them together without a translator.

segments.voice: Whether you're a Buddhist or just learning the sound, say the homage slowly, on one breath if you can, three times: namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa. If you'd like, add the refuges: Buddham saranam gacchami, Dhammam saranam gacchami, Sangham saranam gacchami. Don't worry about every syllable; let the rhythm carry you, then sit in the quiet the chant leaves behind.

1382.title: The Heart Sutra in Japanese
1382.hook: the Heart Sutra chanted fast and steady to a wooden drum in Zen halls
1382.howItsDone: In Japanese Zen temples and in some Zen centers elsewhere, the Heart Sutra is chanted together during services, in Japanese readings of the Chinese text, with a leader striking a wooden fish drum to keep an even beat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chanting in Pali: homage, refuges and reflections, the Theravada morning chant. Your line was chanting in Pali. Back on day 267 you met the Heart Sutra itself; today, its sound in a Zen hall.

Tock. Tock. Tock. In a Zen hall in Japan, a monk strikes a hollow wooden drum in a steady beat, and the whole room chants with it: kan ji zai bo sa, gyo jin han nya ha ra mi ta ji. No melody to speak of. Fast, low, level, one syllable on each stroke. Nobody races ahead; nobody drags behind. A newcomer loses the place within a line and finds it again a few beats later, because the drum never stopped.
screen: `TOCK. TOCK. TOCK.` → `ONE SYLLABLE, ONE STROKE.` → `THE DRUM NEVER STOPS.`

segments.voice: First, the text. The Heart Sutra is a short Mahayana teaching from the family called the Perfection of Wisdom. In it, Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, practicing deep wisdom, sees that the five heaps that make up a person are empty, and explains this to the monk Shariputra: form is emptiness, emptiness is form. Empty, in Mahayana teaching, doesn't mean nothing. It means nothing stands on its own; each thing leans on other things. Second, the sound. Zen halls in Japan chant a Chinese text read aloud in Japanese sounds, so form is emptiness becomes shiki soku ze ku, ku soku ze shiki. The closing mantra, in Sanskrit gate gate paragate parasamgate bodhi svaha, comes out as gya tei, gya tei, ha ra gya tei. Third, the drum. It's a mokugyo, a wooden fish, carved hollow and struck with a padded stick. Tradition says it's a fish because a fish never closes its eyes: a reminder to stay awake. The chant leader keeps the beat, and the room follows. Fourth, why chant it this way. That rhythm leaves no room to admire your own voice, or to plan lunch and still keep up. You don't perform the Heart Sutra; you join it. Some teachers say the meaning is for study at other times; in the hall, the steadiness is the teaching. Some Zen centers in the West chant it in Japanese, some in English, some in both.
screen: `A SHORT TEXT ON EMPTINESS.` · `A CHINESE TEXT IN JAPANESE SOUNDS.` · `THE WOODEN FISH THAT NEVER SLEEPS.` · `YOU DON'T PERFORM IT. YOU JOIN IT.` · then, large: `FORM IS EMPTINESS, EMPTINESS IS FORM.`

segments.voice: Tap your knee or the table with one finger in a slow, even beat, about the pace of a calm walk, and on each tap say one syllable, quietly or in your head: gya tei, gya tei, ha ra gya tei, or simply one, two, three, four. When you lose the words, don't stop tapping; wait for the next beat and step back in.
The Heart Sutra in Japanese. A short Mahayana teaching on emptiness, chanted in Japanese readings of Chinese characters, one syllable to each stroke of a wooden drum. Today's word.

1383.title: The mani sung
1383.hook: Om mani padme hum sung in long tunes in Tibetan homes
1383.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists recite om mani padme hum on prayer beads, sing it to slow tunes at home and at work, carve it on stones, print it inside prayer wheels that they turn as they walk, and print it on flags.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Heart Sutra in Japanese, one syllable to each stroke of a wooden fish. Your line was the drum keeps time. You first met om mani padme hum on day 306; today, you hear it sung.

A pot of butter tea is warming on the stove in a Tibetan kitchen, and the grandmother stirring it is singing under her breath. The tune is long and slow, rising on one syllable, resting on the next, falling back and starting over. Her grandson, doing homework at the table, hums along without looking up. No drum, no hall, no leader. Just a melody that has been in this house longer than the stove, and words she has sung all her life: om mani padme hum.
screen: `BUTTER TEA ON THE STOVE.` → `A LONG, SLOW TUNE.` → `OM MANI PADME HUM.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Om and hum are sacred syllables without a simple translation; the two middle words are usually translated jewel and lotus. Teachers explain the whole in different ways. Some link the jewel to compassion and the lotus to wisdom; some take each syllable as its own door. In Tibetan it's often heard as om mani peme hung. Second, whose words. Tradition ties the mantra to Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion from yesterday's Heart Sutra. In Tibet he is called Chenrezig, and the mani is his. Saying it calls compassion to mind and wishes it for every being, the stranger as much as the grandchild. Third, sung. The mani can be murmured on a string of beads, but at home it is also sung, to long tunes that differ from family to family and region to region: while cooking, walking, rocking a baby, sitting with someone who is ill. A tune can't be hurried. Each syllable stretches, and the breath slows to carry it. Fourth, beyond the voice. The same words are carved into stones piled along paths, called mani stones. They're printed on long scrolls packed inside prayer wheels, which people turn clockwise as they walk; tradition says each turn sends the mantra out as if spoken. They're printed on flags so the wind can carry them. A house, a path, a mountain pass can all be singing the mani at once.

segments.voice: If you'd like, sing om, mani, padme, hum softly to any slow tune that comes, letting each syllable stretch; families sing it many ways, so there's no melody to get wrong. If you'd rather not sing these words, hum one long, low note on each out-breath. Either way, while the sound lasts, bring to mind someone who could use a little kindness today.

1384.title: The name chanted
1384.hook: Namo Amituofo chanted as people walk around a Chinese hall
1384.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists in China and across East Asia recite Amitabha's name, often on beads, and in temple halls they walk in a line around the Buddha image chanting Namo Amituofo, then sit while the recitation continues silently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mani sung: om mani padme hum, to long tunes in Tibetan kitchens. Your line was sung. Today, another short phrase, said with the feet.

What happens to a name when you say it with every step? In a Buddhist hall in China, a line of people in gray robes and ordinary coats moves slowly around the room. Slippers on a wooden floor, hands folded or holding beads. The line curves past a golden figure of a Buddha and around again, everyone saying the same short phrase in a soft, even chant: Namo Amituofo. A step, a syllable, a step. Nobody is going anywhere, and nobody seems in a hurry to stop.
screen: `A NAME WITH EVERY STEP.` → `AROUND THE HALL.` → `NAMO AMITUOFO.`

segments.voice: First, whose name. Amituofo is how Chinese Buddhists say Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light. In the Pure Land sutras, he made vows long ago to create a land where beings could practice without obstacles, and to welcome those who call on him with trust. Pure Land Buddhists, in China and across East Asia, rest their practice on that vow. Second, the words. Namo means homage, or I turn to: a greeting and a turning, homage to Amitabha. Some Chinese Buddhists use the phrase in daily life too, to say hello, thank you, or I'm sorry. Third, the walking. People circle the image of the Buddha, keeping it on their right side, an old Buddhist sign of respect. They chant as they go, slow, sometimes quicker, then slow again. Then they often sit, and the chanting goes on silently, inside. Fourth, why walk. The body walks, the voice chants, and the name gives the mind somewhere to rest. In the shorter Pure Land sutra, the Buddha tells his disciple Shariputra about those who hold the name of Amitabha with an undivided mind. Teachers in this school differ on how much the practice is trust in Amitabha's vow and how much it is steadying the mind; some hold both together. For them, the name isn't a magic word. It's a way of remembering, again and again, with feet and voice.

1385.title: Bowing
1385.hook: bowing in all schools, from a small bow to full prostration
1385.howItsDone: Buddhists bow in their own ways: Zen practitioners bow with palms together, Theravada Buddhists kneel and touch the floor, often three times for the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, and Tibetan Buddhists practice full-length prostrations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the name chanted: Namo Amituofo, said step by step around a Chinese hall. Your line was walking the name. On day 2 you asked why Buddhists bow three times; today, the bow itself.

Soon after his awakening, an old discourse says, the Buddha sat alone and had a surprising thought. It is hard, he reflected, to live without someone to honor and respect. So he looked for someone wiser to bow to. In the whole world, he found no one. So he decided to honor the truth he had awakened to, the Dhamma itself. Even the awakened one, in this story, wanted something to honor.
screen: `JUST AFTER AWAKENING.` → `SOMEONE TO HONOR.` → `HE HONORS THE DHAMMA.`

segments.voice: First, the small bow. Across Buddhist schools, the simplest bow is palms together at the chest and a slight bend forward. Zen calls the folded hands gassho. It greets a teacher, a friend, a meal, a cushion before sitting on it. Second, the kneeling bow. In Theravada temples in places like Thailand and Sri Lanka, people lower forehead, forearms and knees to the floor, often three times: once for the Buddha, once for the Dhamma, once for the Sangha. Children learn it young; adults do it entering a shrine room, before a monk, or before sleep. Third, the full prostration. In Tibetan practice, people stretch the whole body flat on the ground, arms out ahead, then rise and do it again. Some do it daily in a shrine room; some pilgrims travel long roads this way, one body length at a time. Fourth, what a bow is for. Buddhist teachers say a bow is not groveling, and not worship of a statue. It lowers the self: the proudest part of you, the head, touches the same floor as the feet. In Zen, some teachers say that in a true bow there is no one bowing and nothing bowed to. In the Theravada telling, it honors what is worth honoring, as the Buddha himself chose to honor the Dhamma. Different schools, different heights, one movement: down, and back up.

1386.title: The ten-day retreat, day one
1386.hook: what happens: noble silence, early bells, the breath
1386.tomorrow: The ten-day retreat, the hard days
1386.howItsDone: On ten-day meditation retreats, such as those in the tradition of S. N. Goenka, students keep noble silence, rise to a bell before dawn, follow a fixed schedule, and begin by attending to the breath at the nostrils.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bowing, from palms together to the whole body on the floor. Your line was bow. This week, Buddhists chanted in Pali, Japanese, Tibetan and Chinese, then lowered the head. Day 152 asked what a retreat is; now, ten days of one.

The phone goes into an envelope with your name on it. Someone at a folding table smiles and puts it in a box. That evening, after a short talk, a teacher announces that silence begins now. Not just no talking: no notes passed, no waving, no catching anyone's eye across the dining hall. You walk back to a narrow room with a bed and a hook for your coat. The next sound you'll hear is a bell, in the dark, long before the sun.
screen: `THE PHONE IN AN ENVELOPE.` → `SILENCE BEGINS NOW.` → `A BELL IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the silence. Retreats often call it noble silence. In courses taught in the tradition of S. N. Goenka, one well-known form of the ten-day retreat, students agree to keep silent with each other, body as well as voice, for most of the course. The point isn't to be cold. It's to stop performing: no one to explain yourself to, and fewer places for the mind to hide. Second, the bells. A bell wakes the hall before dawn, and bells call people to meditation, meals and rest. The day runs on them, so nobody has to decide what's next. Deciding is one more thing set down. Third, the breath. Day one's instruction is small: feel the breath coming in and going out at the nostrils. Not controlling it, just knowing it. This is very close to the old discourse on mindfulness of breathing, where the Buddha describes a monk going to a quiet place, sitting, and knowing a long breath as long and a short breath as short. Fourth, what day one feels like, by the accounts students give: the mind wanders off everywhere, and the instruction is simply to come back. Teachers on these courses say that isn't failing the practice. Coming back is the practice. The ten-day retreat starts with almost nothing: no phone, no talking, and the air at the tip of the nose.
